# Cyclistic Bike-Share Analysis: Converting Casual Riders to Members

## Business Task:

Cyclistic is a Chicago-based bike-share company that has grown a fleet of 5824 bicycles across 692 stations in Chicago. Until now, their marketing strategy focused on general awareness and appealing to the general consumer by providing 3 pricing levels: single-ride passes, day passes, and annual passes. Cyclistic sets itself apart by also offering reclining bikes, hand tricycles, and cargo bikes, making bike-share more inclusive to people with disabilities and riders who can’t use a standard two-wheeled bike. The majority of riders opt for traditional bikes; about 8% of riders use the assistive options. Cyclistic users are more likely to ride for leisure, but about 30% use the bikes to commute to work each day. Financial Analysis has revealed that the annual pass is considerably more profitable than casual members (single and day pass riders). The Director of Marketing at Cyclistic (Lily Moreno) has determined that maximizing the number of annual riders will be key to future growth. Rather than attempting to convert new members to annual, Moreno believes there is ample opportunity to convert casual riders to annual riders. 

To that end, Moreno has defined a clear goal: Design marketing strategies aimed at converting casual riders into annual members. In order to do that, however, the team needs to better understand how annual members and casual riders differ, why casual riders would buy a membership, and how digital media could affect their marketing tactics. Moreno and her team are interested in analyzing the Cyclistic historical bike trip data to identify trends. 

As part of that team, I have been asked to provide a potential answer to the following question: 

**Identify how annual members and casual riders use Cyclistic bikes differently to inform a targeted marketing strategy aimed at converting casual riders into annual members** 

The insights that I will provide will help Lily Moreno and the Marketing Analytics Team better understand the trends and differences between casual and annual riders and therefore make better data-driven decisions for how to adjust and create the marketing campaign for converting casual riders to annual riders. 

### Relevant Stakeholders:

* Lily Moreno (Director of Marketing and my Manager)  
* Cyclistic Marketing Analytics Team  
* Cyclistic Executive Team

# Preparation

### Data Source & Description 

The data used for this analysis includes a total of 6 months of Cyclistic historical trip data across two quarterly datasets (Q1 2019 and Q1 2020), provided by Motive International Inc. The datasets are sourced as individual quarterly CSV files.

### Data organization & content 

The dataset contains individual rows for each logged ride with the following key attributes. 

| Category | Column name (header) | Description | Data type |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Ride identifier | ride\_id | Individual unique ID code for each ride | object |
| Time stamps | started\_at | Starting timestamp | datetime |
|  | ended\_at | Ending timestamp | datetime |
| Station identifiers | start \_station\_name | Name of departure station | object |
|  | start\_station\_id | Identifier code for departure station | int64 |
|  | end\_station\_name | Name of arrival station | object |
|  | end\_station\_id | Identifier code for arrival station | int64 |
| User type | usertype | The type of user for each ride, casual (normal customer), and member (annual subscriber) | object |

### Data Credibility and Integrity

Data credibility and integrity has been evaluated based on the ROCCC principle. 

* Reliable and Original: The trip data is provided directly by Motivate International Inc. (the system operator). Each bike is geotracked and locked into a network of 692 physical stations across Chicago. The resulting data is managed directly under Motivate’s dataset license; it represents primary, first-party data rather than survey estimates.   
* Comprehensive: The data includes system-logged rides occurring within Q1 2019 and Q1 2020, capturing full operational volume for both target quarters   
* Current: comparing identical first-quarter timeframes across two consecutive years provides a multi-year baseline to evaluate how rider behavior and member-to-casual user ratios shifted over time. This specific time-frame captures a major transition window in cyclistic’s reporting system providing a real-world case study in aligning divergent data schemas across multi-year operational datasets.   
* Cited: The public data used in this project is licensed under the Motivate International Inc. dataset license agreement. 

### Privacy and Security: 

Data privacy constraints prohibit the use of personally identifiable information (PII) to be included in the provided data. Consequently, Individual riders cannot be tracked across multiple pass purchases or linked to specific credit cards or home addresses. 

### Analytical limitations and risk mitigations

* Data privacy constraints limit our ability to track rides per user; to mitigate this, we’ve chosen to use trip volume characteristics (e.g., duration, time of day) rather than per individual  
* Between 2019 and 2020, Cyclistic began using a different methodology to track their individual bikes. In 2019, each bike was given a singular numeric ID; in 2020, they began defining bike type by its rideable type (docked, electric, classic) because of this, we are unable to aggregate our data according to rideable type and will need to forego this column. 

# Data Processing

## Tool Selection

For the purposes of this case study I chose to utilize a mixture of Excel and Python with Google Colab as the Python environment, leveraging the pandas and numpy libraries for data manipulation.

The datasets had notable differences in their column headers and data structures, which necessitated data transformation before merging into a singular dataset. Given the size of the chosen datasets (\~400k rows each), Python was chosen to quickly and efficiently manipulate the data while maintaining data integrity. Python (while using the pandas and numpy libraries) allowed for this study to maintain data conformity and quickly create additional calculated fields using the new consistent data. 

## Data Consolidation and Alignment

*Chosen datasets:*

For the purposes of this study, the Divvy\_trips\_Q1\_2019 and Divvy\_trips\_Q1\_2020 csv files were chosen from the Motive International Inc. Database. 

*Data Differences*

There were several notable differences in the two individual files. As there was a shift in trip recording conventions for Cyclistic between 2019 and 2020 these differences include but are not limited to the following: 

* Column differences  
  * trip\_id vs ride\_id  
  * start\_time vs started\_at   
  * usertype vs member\_casual  
* Bike type differences  
  * During 2019, Cyclistic recorded each bike type by providing each bike an individual ID, while in 2020 bike\_id’s were foregone in favor of bike status “Docked\_bike”, this rendered these columns unusable as their data does not exist in the other. 

*Remedies*

Before combining the datasets, the raw schema and data types of the Q1 2019 and Q1 2020 datasets were inspected and compared; data types were then changed to align to the 2020 file. 

To align the headers across both datasets, the following key column renames were executed in Python: 

| Original Column name | New column name |
| :---- | :---- |
| Trip\_id | ride\_id |
| start\_time | started\_at |
| end\_time | ended\_at |
| from\_station\_name | start\_station\_name |
| from\_station\_id | start\_station\_id |
| to\_station\_name | end\_station\_name |
| to\_station\_id | end\_station\_id |

After standardization, the two quarterly datasets were concatenated into a single unified dataframe containing individual rows for each ride in Q1 2019 and Q1 2020, with shared columns containing no missing data for any row. 

The Rideable\_type column was found to be an invalid column, with the data from 2020 representing a different recording convention than the 2019 data. For this reason, the column was removed from our data in order to avoid potential analysis errors. 

## Feature Engineering

New variables were created in order to promote deeper analysis of the data. 

These calculated fields were:

| New Column Name | description | calcuation | Data type |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| date | Reported date (DD:MM:YYYY) of a given ride  | Extracted from “started\_at” column | object |
| day | Reported numerical weekday of a given ride | Extracted from “started\_at” column | int32 |
| month | Reported month of a given ride | Extracted from “started\_at” column | int32 |
| year | Reported year of a given ride | Extracted from “started\_at” column | int32 |
| weekday | Reported weekday of a given ride | Extracted from “started\_at” column | object |
| ride\_length | The length of a given ride (in seconds) | Calculated by subtracting the “started\_at” time from the “ended\_at” time of each row | float64 |
| ride\_length\_minutes | The length of a given ride (in minutes) | Calculated by dividing each time in “ride\_length” by 60 | float64 |

## Data Cleaning and Integrity

To ensure accuracy of the data, a few steps were taken to remove “bad data”; firstly, a number of the entries were arrivals of bikes to Cyclistic HQ for repair. These rides were performed by employees and were therefore removed in order to confirm our limitation of ride data to users only. 

Secondly, upon inspection, some of the calculated ride lengths were negative; these rows were also removed to ensure there were no invalid data entries. 

Lastly, a check for duplicate and blank rows was conducted using Python methods, confirming zero duplicates or blanks post-consolidation and thereby confirming data integrity. 

| Audit table |  |  |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Cleaning step | Rows affected/ dropped | Remaining rows |
| Initial raw concatenation | \- | 791956 |
| Removed HQ repairs and  negative / zero ride\_length’s  | 3767 | 788189 |
| Removed missing null values | \- | 788189 |

# Analysis

## Organization & Formatting

Our post-cleaning dataset comprises 788189 rows, which, when examined as a whole, do not provide significant insight into our business task. However, after grouping the data into meaningful buckets according to user type, day of the week, or month, we began to see meaningful differences between the casual and annual members, giving us actionable answers to our business question.

Prior to this grouping, I confirmed that my data was formatted correctly (ride\_length & ride\_length\_minutes as float64 in minutes and seconds, timestamps formatted as datetimes, etc.) Once this confirmation was complete, I grouped the data meaningfully. For the purpose of the analysis, I chose to use the calculated field of ride length in minutes for easier interpretation. 

## Summary & Descriptive statistics

An initial calculation of the mean, median, max, and min for the ride length in minutes, grouped by user type (casual or annual members), resulted in the following data:

| User type | Mean | Median | Max | Min | Total rides |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Casual | 89.54 | 23.21 | 177,200 | 0.033 | 67877 |
| Member | 13.25 | 8.4 | 101607 | 0.0167 | 720312 |

Note: the max ride duration for casual members is one of 4 rides that exceeded 100k minutes and is likely skewing the mean higher. 

At first glance, this data seemingly shows that although the initial provided context fo rthis case showed that only 30% of users used the bikes for commuting to work and that the majority of Cyclistic users utilized their bikes to perform frequent long leisure rides, we see here that Annual members actually performed shorter rides on average when compared to casual riders. This information proved rather surprising, prompting me to question the initial context and adjust our hypothesis. 

When attempting other groupings of the data. I began by examining the difference in the ride lengths of the users grouped by day of the week, and found that while members perform shorter rides than casual riders on average, I saw that both casual and annual members had a significant drop in ride length on weekend days (Saturday and Sunday). This information showed me that the data required further examination. 

## Trends & Behavioral Discoveries 

Upon examining the number of rides performed per day of the day, I found that members primarily ride during the workweek, with roughly half the number of rides on weekends (Data shown in table below). Based on this discovery, I adjusted my hypothesis to “For what purpose do Cyclistic users utilize their passes” 

| User type | Sunday | Monday | Tuesday | Wednesday | Thursday | Friday | Saturday |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| casual | 18652 | 5591 | 7311 | 7690 | 7147 | 8013 | 13473 |
| member | 60197 | 110430 | 127974 | 121902 | 125228 | 115168 | 59413 |

*Table shown above: Rows: split by usertype. Columns are split by day of the week, and values show the number of rides on a given day by usertype.* 

This data supports the notion that annual members of Cyclistic use their rides as transportation to and from work, while casual riders can use it for that purpose as well; the length of their rides suggests that the rides are more likely for enjoyment, exercise, or relaxation. 

To try to strengthen this possible explanation, I chose to inspect the number of rides per hour for our two user types. This showed that while rides for casual riders peak around 5 pm during weekdays, annual members, however, peak between 6- 9 am and 4- 7 pm during weekdays. Along with this, it was found that casual riders and annual members have similar distributions of their start times during weekends, with annual members still performing significantly more rides. This finding strengthens our new hypothesis that annual members use their rides for transportation to and from work, as the data show their rides tend to start at the beginning and end of the workday. 

*To see the distribution of the number of rides per hour split by time of the week and user type. with bar labels represent the average duration of rides at that time. please view the image connected to this repository*

As we see here, the average duration of rides for annual members stays significantly lower than for casual riders. This aligns with the theory that Annual riders' usage differs from casual riders' usage, as annual members use Cyclistic bikes for short commutes while Casual riders use them for leisure. 

# Conclusion

In conclusion, based on the analysis of the Cyclistic Historical trip data for Q1 2019 and Q1 2020, annual riders differ from casual riders in three key ways. Firstly, annual riders primarily use the bikes for quick rides (under 20 minutes on average), while casual riders use Cyclistic bikes for long rides (89 minutes on average). Secondly, during the standard work week  (Monday-Friday) annual riders use Cyclistic bikes primarily during rush hour (6-9 AM, 5-7 PM), while casual riders peak once throughout the day, typically between 2-4 PM. Thirdly, the number of rides for annual and casual members have reversed trends. With casual riders using the service more on Sundays and saturdays while annual members use the services less on those days. These differences suggest that annual riders primarily use Cyclistic bikes for their commute to and from work, while casual riders use them for leisurely rides. 

Because casual riders are already familiar with the Cyclistic brand and system, converting them into annual members represents a cost-effective path to driving long-term revenue growth. However, because casual riders ride primarily for leisure rather than daily commuting, marketing campaigns must reframe the value proposition of an annual membership around leisure convenience and cost savings 

## Recommendations

Based on the findings in this study, I would suggest the following actions:

1. Targeted Weekend & Seasonal Conversion Campaigns  
   1. Casual rider activity surges dramatically on weekends (Saturday/Sunday) and during peak leisure hours. I suggest deploying targeted digital advertising (geofenced mobile ads near high-traffic casual start stations, parks, and waterfronts) during peak weekend daylight hours and focusing campaign messaging on weekend freedom, recurring recreational use, and the long-term value of an annual pass. 	

2. Introduce a "Weekend / Leisure" Tier or Tiered Membership Perk  
   1. Casual riders take significantly longer rides per session (\~89 minutes vs. \~13 minutes for members). Standard annual memberships targeting daily commuters may not appeal to users who only ride on weekends. Perhaps Cyclistic should consider introducing a specialized or seasonal membership option (e.g., a "Weekend Warrior" pass or a discounted summer annual pass). Alternatively, structure the main membership marketing to highlight how taking just 2–3 long weekend rides per month makes an annual membership cheaper than paying full single-ride or day-pass rates.

### Recommended next steps for further data collection 

* **Collect Anonymized Survey Data:** Conduct targeted digital surveys at casual-heavy stations to capture demographic data, user intent (tourism vs. resident leisure), and perceived barriers to purchasing an annual pass.

* **Implement Anonymized User Tracking:** Work with the engineering team to assign unique, privacy-compliant rider tokens (without storing payment details or PII) to track how frequently specific casual riders return. This will identify "power casuals" who are ripe for membership conversion.
